title: Signature Solution - Planning
summary: Students plan a five-part signature solution - goal, prompt structure, inputs, evaluation method and risk plan - and take it through an approve-to-build gate.
objectives: Plan a structured AI solution: state the goal, the prompt structure, and the check steps.
Identify the inputs/data and the output-evaluation method.
Describe one risk and how the plan reduces it.

body: Today you become a designer, not just a prompter. Before anyone types a single word into an AI tool, you will plan a small solution with five parts that fit together: a goal, a prompt structure, inputs, a check, and a risk plan. A good plan is like a bridge design drawn before the first bolt is placed - it lets you find weak spots on paper, where fixing them is cheap.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can state the goal of my solution in one clear sentence.
I can lay out a prompt structure with a role, a task, and one rule.
I can name the inputs my solution needs and how I will check the output.
I can describe one risk and one way my plan reduces it.

terms.definition: A small, reusable AI design with a clear goal and connected parts that solves one simple task.
The shape of a prompt: a role for the AI, a clear task, and at least one rule or limit.
The information a prompt works on, chosen to contain no personal or identifying data.
The agreed way you will judge whether an output is accurate.
A design choice that lowers the chance or impact of something going wrong.

sections.heading: From one prompt to a whole solution
body: In Grade 5 you improved a single prompt. This term you design a solution: a set of parts that work together to do one simple job well.
The five parts are the goal, the [[prompt structure]], the inputs, the [[evaluation method]], and the risk plan. If any part is missing, the solution is harder to trust.

sections.heading: Writing a prompt structure
body: A [[prompt structure]] names a role ('You are a timetable helper'), a task ('list the three earliest buses'), and one rule ('if a time is missing, say so').
The role focuses the AI, the task says exactly what to do, and the rule keeps the output honest and easy to check.

sections.heading: Checks and risks before you build
body: An [[evaluation method]] says how you will judge accuracy, such as comparing the output to a known-correct answer key.

A risk plan names one thing that could go wrong, like a confident wrong answer, and one design choice that reduces it, like a 'say if unsure' rule plus a human check. Never put personal or identifying data into a prompt.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will now plan your own signature solution on the plan sheet. You will not log in to any tool; the teacher runs any AI on the board. Your job is to make the plan complete and safe.
items: Read your task card and write the goal in one clear sentence.
Fill the role-task-rule slots for your prompt structure.
List the inputs your prompt needs, checking there is no personal data.
Write your evaluation method and one risk with its mitigation.
Self-check against the five-part list, then submit for the approve-to-build gate.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which part of a plan is easiest to forget, and why does that matter?
How does a 'say if unsure' rule make an output safer to trust?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one part of your plan you are most confident about.
Write the one part you will strengthen before building next week.

worksheet.title: Week 7 - Core - Worksheet | Signature Solution - Planning

questions.prompt: Layla planned a lost-property helper. Goal: "Sort the found-items list into categories so items get back to their owners faster." Prompt structure: "You are a lost-property helper. Sort each item into clothing, devices or other. If an item does not fit a category, label it other." Inputs: "a made-up list of ten found items, with no names on it." Risk: "the AI might put an item in the wrong category, so a person reads the sorted list before it is posted." Which one of the five plan parts is still missing?

options.text: The evaluation method - she has not said how she will judge whether the sorting is accurate.
The goal - her first sentence does not say what the solution is for.
The inputs - she has not said what information the prompt works on.
The risk mitigation - she names a risk but does nothing about it.

feedback.correct: Right - Layla has a risk plan but no agreed way to judge accuracy, such as checking the sorted list against a teacher's answer key.
feedback.incorrect: Look again: the goal, the inputs and a mitigation (a person checks before posting) are all there. Nothing tells you how she will judge whether the sorting is accurate.

questions.prompt: Omar wrote these five lines on his plan sheet for a bus-timetable helper. Match each line to the part of the plan it fills.

left.text: "Help new students find the three earliest buses home after clubs."
"You are a timetable helper. List the three earliest buses. If a time is missing, say so."
"A made-up timetable of twelve bus times, with no student names on it."
"I will compare the three times the AI lists against the teacher's answer key."
"The AI might invent a bus time, so a person checks the three times before they go on the noticeboard."

feedback.correct: Well matched - a plan is complete when all five parts are written down and each one does its own job.
feedback.incorrect: Check the last two: the evaluation method says how you judge accuracy, while the risk mitigation names something that could go wrong and the choice that reduces it.

questions.prompt: Sara says: "My risk plan already says a person will check the output, so I do not need an evaluation method as well." Is Sara right?

feedback.correct: Correct - the evaluation method tells that person what to compare the output against, so without it the check has no standard to judge by.
feedback.incorrect: The two parts do different jobs: the evaluation method sets how accuracy is judged (for example, against an answer key), and the risk plan lowers the chance or impact of a failure.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the plan-sheet routine into the order the lesson gives them.

items.text: Read the task card and write the goal in one clear sentence.
Fill the role, task and rule slots of the prompt structure.
List the inputs the prompt needs, checking there is no personal data.
Write the evaluation method and one risk with its mitigation.
Self-check against the five-part list, then submit for the approve-to-build gate.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the goal comes first because every later part has to serve it, and the gate comes last because it checks a finished plan.
feedback.incorrect: The goal is written first, the prompt structure and inputs are built to serve it, the check and risk come next, and the approve-to-build gate is the last step.

questions.prompt: Rashid's solution sorts a found-items list. The risk he names is: "the AI might add an item that was never on my list, and sound sure about it." Choose the TWO design choices in his plan that would reduce that risk.

options.text: Add the rule: "Use only the items on the list I give you. If you are unsure about an item, say so."
Check the sorted list against the original found-items list before anything is posted.
Make the goal sentence longer so the AI is given more detail to work with.
Give the AI twenty items at a time instead of ten so it has more to compare.
Ask the AI to sound more confident so the sorted list is easier to read.

feedback.correct: Yes - a rule that limits the AI to the given items plus a human check against the original list both make an invented item far less likely to slip through.
feedback.incorrect: A longer goal, a bigger batch or a more confident tone do not stop an invented item. What stops it is a rule that ties the AI to your list and a check against that list.

formative.targets: Checks planning of the signature solution against the Emerging project criteria
formative.check: Plan review against the project rubric (Emerging); approve-to-build gate
formative.successCriteria: Plan states goal, prompt structure, inputs, an evaluation method, and one risk mitigation.
